newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - Michelin pumps up pre-exceptional profit.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Michelin pumps up pre-exceptional profit.

text.p: Tyremaker Michelin said on Tuesday that profit excluding tax and exceptional items rose 50 percent to 2.88 billion francs ($561 million) in the first six months of the year, boosted by higher sales and lower production costs.
Net profit, however, fell 10 percent to 1.35 billion francs in the first half after Michelin took a 709 million franc charge to restructure its Spanish subsidiary to cut its costs further.
Investors focused on the big underlying profit gains and drove the share price up 1.96 percent to 265.20 francs.
"They were very good figures. Brokers are upgrading (their recommendations)...the message is very positive," a trader said.
Michelin's operating profit rose 31 percent to 3.62 billion francs, helped by productivity gains and tyre price increases set last year after rubber prices soared.
Finance Director Eric Bourdais de Charbonniere told a news conference raw materials prices had fallen four percent in the first half and the benefits would show up in the second half.
The first-half results were also helped by lower interest rates, which reduced Michelin's financial expenses even though its debt grew because of a sudden buildup in inventories.
"We overestimated the demand in Europe, particularly in trucks," Bourdais de Charbonniere said.
Michelin is the world's second largest-tyremaker after Japan's Bridgestone, according to the Tire Business trade journal.
The French company's sales rose 5.4 percent to 34.91 billion francs as growth in Asian and Latin American sales offset weakness in the European and U.S. markets.
It has 18 percent of the global market in car, truck, airplane, tractor and other tyres, compared with Bridgestone's 19 percent and U.S. company Goodyear's 15 percent.

The company declined to give a profit forecast but Bourdais de Charbonniere said it did not dispute analysts' estimates, compiled before the first-half results and exceptional charge, for a profit between three and 3.5 billion francs.
Several analysts said they would probably cut their earnings forecasts for 1996 to take into account the exceptional first-half charge but raise their estimates for 1997.

"The operating results were a lot better than expected," said analyst Nick Snee at JP Morgan. "The fact that they're pressing ahead with restructuring is a good thing. You don't worry about restructuring charges."
Paris brokerage Cheuvreux de Virieu added Michelin to its list of recommended stocks on Tuesday.
For most analysts, the blot on Michelin's first-half results was the rise in its debt to 23.2 billion francs at the end of June from 21.6 billion a year earlier.
Bourdais de Charbonniere said the group had slowed production to pare its inventories and its debt at the end of August was below August 1995 levels "so we're moving in the right direction".

He said long-term objectives include a desire to expand in Asia to take advantage of the growth potential -- particularly for truck tyres, as road transport represents a bigger share of transport in emerging economies than in developed ones.
Further geographic diversification dovetails with Michelin's aim to reduce the earnings fluctuations mirroring those of its highly cyclical customers, the car and truck industries.
Its exposure to the European industry cycle has been reduced by its important U.S. activities, including Goodrich, which generate a third of Michelin's turnover. Europe still accounts for 55 percent.
($1=5.137 French Franc)
